answer.question: Why did Kubernetes move to three releases per year?
answer.answer: Kubernetes changed from four to three releases per year (a KEP merged on April 23, 2021, formalizing a cadence that had started ad hoc in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic, when SIG Release extended the 1.19 cycle to lessen the burden on contributors and end users). The reasons given in the evidence: (1) As the project matures, the number of enhancements per cycle grows, increasing the burden on contributors and the Release Engineering team, and downstream consumers and integrators struggle to keep up with ever more feature-packed releases; wider adoption means a bigger downstream chain is affected. (2) Three releases balance stakeholder needs: consumers get longer support terms per minor version (the previous three releases are supported for longer, though it is not strictly an LTS policy), and contributors get more time to mature enhancements and make them production-ready. (3) Management overhead for SIG Release and Release Engineering diminishes, letting them focus on release quality and tooling. (4) The KEP also says fewer releases leave more room for triage, development, conferences and release preparation, giving better planning and predictability. The 1.22 changelog adds that the release team listened to its user base about the number of releases per year. The 1.22 and 1.23 cycles were each planned at 15 weeks.

answer.question: What enforces pod security standards in-tree?
answer.answer:
The built-in Pod Security admission controller (Pod Security Admission, the `PodSecurity` admission plugin) enforces the Pod Security Standards in-tree. It is stable (GA) since v1.25 and enabled by default. It replaces the removed PodSecurityPolicy.

Restrictions are applied at the namespace level when pods are created. You set them with namespace labels for the privileged, baseline and restricted levels. Each label can be applied in enforce, audit or warn mode.

You can set cluster-wide defaults and exemptions with a `PodSecurityConfiguration` passed via `--admission-control-config-file` to kube-apiserver. Exemptions can be by username, RuntimeClass or namespace.

answer.question: What happens to unused auto-generated ServiceAccount token Secrets?
answer.answer: Unused auto-generated legacy ServiceAccount token Secrets are first invalidated and later deleted by the legacy ServiceAccount token cleaner (feature LegacyServiceAccountTokenCleanUp), which runs in kube-controller-manager and checks every 24 hours. It relies on the ConfigMap the control plane creates when LegacyServiceAccountTokenTracking is enabled (kube-apiserver-legacy-service-account-token-tracking); if that ConfigMap is unavailable, no secret is removed. Once the configured period has passed since the date in the ConfigMap, the cleaner evaluates each Secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token. A Secret is marked invalid if it meets all of these conditions: it is auto-generated (bi-directionally referenced by a ServiceAccount), it is not mounted by any pod, and it has not been used for the specified period since creation or last use. Marking means adding the label kubernetes.io/legacy-token-invalid-since with the current date. If the invalid Secret then stays unused for the period again, the cleaner deletes it. The period defaults to one year and can be set with the kube-controller-manager flag --legacy-service-account-token-clean-up-period. This behavior applies from version 1.29. If someone uses an invalidated token, the validator adds the audit annotation authentication.k8s.io/legacy-token-invalidated, increments the invalid_legacy_auto_token_uses_total metric, updates the kubernetes.io/legacy-token-last-used label, and returns an error. Users can remove the kubernetes.io/legacy-token-invalid-since label to temporarily allow the token again, or switch to the TokenRequest API.

answer.question: Did Kubernetes create a token Secret for every ServiceAccount?
answer.answer: Yes, but only in older releases. Before version 1.24, Kubernetes automatically generated Secret-based tokens for ServiceAccounts. Starting in 1.24, the `LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration` feature gate was beta and enabled by default. With it on, Secret objects holding service account tokens are no longer auto-generated for every ServiceAccount; the token controller stops creating them. Instead, you get tokens from the TokenRequest API. If you need a non-expiring token, you create a Secret yourself for the token controller to populate. From 1.29 onward, leftover auto-generated legacy tokens are marked invalid if unused for a set period (one year by default). If they stay unused for a further such period, the control plane purges them.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes stop auto-generating Secret-based ServiceAccount tokens?
answer.answer: According to KEP-2799's motivation, once BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume went GA in 1.22, Pods got their service account tokens through the TokenRequest API, stored as a projected volume. The docs describe the advantage of the newer tokens: they have bounded lifetimes and are automatically invalidated when the Pod they are mounted into is deleted. The 1.29 release blog gives the same account: Kubernetes had switched by 1.22 to more secure tokens that are time-limited and bound to specific Pods, then stopped auto-generating legacy Secret-based tokens in 1.24. The 1.24 changelog confirms that from then on such Secrets are no longer auto-generated for every ServiceAccount. Users should get tokens from the TokenRequest API, or manually create a Secret if they need a non-expiring token.

answer.question: Does the API server reject IP addresses with leading zeros by default?
answer.answer:
Yes, as of release 1.37. The StrictIPCIDRValidation feature gate has been beta and enabled by default since 1.36. With it on, IPv4 addresses with leading zeros (e.g. `010.000.000.005`) are rejected, along with CIDR values that contain such IPs. IPv4-mapped IPv6 values and ambiguous CIDR subnet/mask values are rejected too.

The rule has limits. It covers only fields in built-in API kinds. It does not cover custom resource kinds, values in Kubernetes configuration files, or command-line arguments.

How this changed over time:
- In 1.23, Kubernetes deliberately kept accepting leading zeros for compatibility.
- In 1.33–1.35, the gate was alpha and off by default. The API server then only warned that such values would be rejected in the future.
- KEP-4858 claims the feature is stable, but the observed stage at 1.37 is beta. The observed stage wins.

answer.answer: Before StrictIPCIDRValidation was on by default (alpha and off by default in 1.33–1.35; beta and on by default from 1.36), Kubernetes still accepted IPv4 addresses with leading zeros. answer.question: Why did Kubernetes tighten validation of IP addresses and CIDRs in API fields?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes historically validated IP and CIDR strings in API fields too loosely. It accepted anything Go's `net.ParseIP` and `net.ParseCIDR` would parse, even though some of those strings had ambiguous meanings that could lead to security problems.

Go 1.17 changed how it handles IPv4 addresses with leading "0"s, to avoid CVE-2021-29923. After that, there was consensus that API validation should eventually become stricter too. This was not done right away because the project did not want to retroactively invalidate existing API objects; KEP-4858 sets out the plan to finally do it.

The specific worry is that different components can read the same string as different IP addresses. Examples are IPv4 octets with leading zeros and IPv4-mapped IPv6 values such as `::ffff:192.168.0.1`. With the `StrictIPCIDRValidation` gate enabled, both forms are rejected.

The stated goals are:
- to avoid security problems from ambiguously-parsable IPs and CIDRs;
- to make such values impossible in the future, at least in new clusters;
- per the v1.36 blog, to catch malformed addresses and prefixes that cause subtle configuration bugs in Services, Pods, NetworkPolicies and other resources.

The KEP claims stable, but the feature-gate reference shows the gate as beta at 1.37 (on by default since 1.36); the observed beta stage takes precedence.

answer.answer: For Kubernetes 1.19 and newer, each minor release receives approximately one year of patch support; releases 1.18 and older got about 9 months. What this means for end users

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes extend patch support for minor releases from 9 months to about a year?
answer.answer:
According to KEP-1498, the support period was extended mainly to meet a request from end users. Business cycles (financial, certification, sales, vacation, HR and others) are overwhelmingly annual, so many users wanted support cycles of at least a year. A 9-month window was an irregular period compared with how most companies plan, operate and budget. It forced operators to upgrade at least every 9 months, and with a new minor release every three months they constantly had to evaluate, plan and move forward on features, deprecations and version skew.

A survey by WG LTS in early 2019 showed that a significant subset of users did not upgrade within the 9-month window. About a third had production machines on versions that were already out of support. The responses suggested that these roughly 30% of users could stay on supported versions if patch support lasted 12-14 months. That would raise the share of users on supported versions from 50-60% to more than 80%, whether they ran DIY builds or vendor distributions. A yearly period gives users the cushion they appear to want and fits familiar annual planning cycles.

The project also saw extending the window toward a year as a relatively minor change. It was considered viable to implement and a meaningful first response to users. Keeping the change small would let the project discover and address the unknowns of changing support windows.

The proposal set 14 months: essentially 12 months of support plus a 2-month upgrade period. This formalized the existing practice of keeping patch branch CI running for 6-7 weeks beyond the 9 months, as a failsafe for critical CVEs or blocking upgrade issues. Release 1.19 and newer get this year of support.

answer.question: Can I write an RBAC rule that explicitly denies a permission?
answer.answer: No. RBAC permissions are purely additive: a Role or ClusterRole holds rules that grant permissions, and there are no "deny" rules. heading_path: Migration from command line arguments to configuration file

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes add a structured authentication configuration file instead of keeping the --oidc-* flags?
answer.answer:
The --oidc-* flags were not simply dropped. The blogs say the command-line options keep working and are still supported. SIG Auth recommends the config file, but you cannot combine it with the flags: setting --authentication-config together with any --oidc-* flag makes the API server report an error and exit (43794, 43797, 17552).

The stated reasons for adding a config file are that the flag-based OIDC authenticator could not give users the customization they wanted. KEP-3331's goals list these limits (17974, 17549):
- Claim validation was only by audience, and only by exact value.
- Claim mapping could only pick a single value from a single top-level claim and prefix groups.
- Using more than one OIDC provider or client ID required an external multiplexing provider such as Dex.
- Changing authenticator settings required restarting kube-apiserver.
- There was no way to apply validation rules to the final user info object.

The KEP also aimed for easy migration from the existing flags.

The blogs add that a file gives more flexibility and extensibility than command-line options and makes it easier to deliver later improvements (43794, 43797). The benefits they list are multiple JWT authenticators, dynamic reload without restarting, CEL-based claim validation and mapping, multiple audiences, and support for providers without OIDC discovery (43795). The v1.34 blog also cites better manageability and auditability of authentication settings (45854).

The KEP considered alternatives: investing in external software like Dex, or adding no more OIDC customization. Its own reasoning on some related design choices is left as a TODO (18030).

The two blogs disagree about when the alpha arrived: one says v1.29, the other says v1.30. Both are tier 6, so this is unresolved, and it does not affect the rationale above.

answer.question: Is kube-proxy's ipvs mode still supported, and what should I use instead?
answer.answer:
As of 1.37, ipvs mode still works but is deprecated, and has been since v1.35. It is only available on Linux nodes. Since 1.35, kube-proxy logs a warning when run in ipvs mode, and kubeadm now adds a delayed deprecation warning too.

The removal timeline:
- **v1.40:** ipvs will be disabled by default. You can re-enable it with the `KubeProxyIPVS` feature gate. Without that override, kube-proxy will exit with an error listing the valid modes (iptables and nftables).
- **v1.43:** ipvs mode will be removed entirely.

What to use instead:
- **nftables mode** is the recommended replacement. It went GA in 1.33, is meant to replace both iptables and ipvs, and performs better than either.
- **iptables mode** is the option if your Linux kernel is too old for nftables. It is still the default, and its performance has improved greatly since ipvs was introduced.

The documentation says ipvs never correctly implemented all Service edge cases. The deprecation KEP adds that sig-network lacks maintainers familiar with the ipvs code. It also notes that all kernels too old for nftables mode will be out of LTS by the end of 2026.

answer.question: Should a new controller watch Endpoints or EndpointSlices to find a Service's backends?
answer.answer:
A new controller should watch EndpointSlices. The Endpoints API has been officially deprecated since v1.33, and the docs recommend that all clients use the EndpointSlice API rather than Endpoints.

The docs give these reasons Endpoints falls short:
- It does not support dual-stack clusters.
- It lacks information needed for newer features such as trafficDistribution.
- It truncates the endpoint list when it is too long for one object.

The v1.33 blog post adds that the API server returns warnings to users who read or write Endpoints. It also says the plan in KEP-4974 is to stop requiring that clusters run the Endpoints controller. That controller might therefore not be running, so Endpoints objects may not exist at all.

When consuming EndpointSlices, note that one Service can have many of them. You find them with the label selector kubernetes.io/service-name=<service>. Expect multiple slices in three main cases:
- One slice per IP family in dual-stack Services.
- Separate slices for endpoints that target different ports.
- Splitting once a Service has more than 100 endpoints.

One side conflict, which does not change this recommendation: the KEP-752 test plan says only Endpoints with the skip label set to "true" are mirrored. The current docs say Endpoints are mirrored unless the skip-mirror label is "true". The docs (tier 1) win over the KEP (tier 3).

answer.question: In Kubernetes 1.20, how did you turn on IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack networking?
answer.answer:
In 1.20, dual-stack was not on by default: you enabled the `IPv6DualStack` feature gate on the relevant components and gave them dual-stack cluster network assignments.

- **kube-apiserver:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"` and `--service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`.
- **kube-controller-manager:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`, `--cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>` and `--service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`. The `--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv4` / `--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv6` flags default to /24 for IPv4 and /64 for IPv6.
- **kubelet:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`.
- **kube-proxy:** `--cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>` and `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`.

The prerequisites were:
- Kubernetes 1.20 or later.
- Provider support for routable IPv4/IPv6 node interfaces.
- A network plugin that supports dual-stack, such as Kubenet or Calico.

In 1.20, dual-stack had been reimplemented to support dual-stack Services. The release notes said it was expected to progress from alpha to beta and GA in coming releases. From 1.21 the feature became beta and enabled by default, so the gate step only applies to 1.20.

answer.question: In Kubernetes 1.20, how could a Service prefer endpoints on the same node as the client?
answer.answer:
In 1.20 you use the alpha Service Topology feature (alpha since v1.17). With it enabled, you set the `topologyKeys` field on the Service spec. This field is a preference-ordered list of Node labels used to sort endpoints. Traffic goes to a Node whose value for the first label matches the originating Node's value, and later labels are tried if there is no match.

To prefer same-node endpoints but still fall back to any endpoint, put `"kubernetes.io/hostname"` first and the catch-all `"*"` last:

```yaml
topologyKeys:
  - "kubernetes.io/hostname"
  - "*"
```

If you use only `["kubernetes.io/hostname"]`, traffic is restricted to same-node endpoints. When none exist on that node, connections fail, as if the Service had no backends.

You can also add intermediate fallbacks after the hostname key and before `"*"`:

```yaml
topologyKeys:
  - "kubernetes.io/hostname"
  - "topology.kubernetes.io/zone"
  - "topology.kubernetes.io/region"
  - "*"
```

If `topologyKeys` is unset or empty, no topology constraints apply.

answer.question: When did kube-proxy's nftables mode become generally available, and what came before?
answer.answer:
kube-proxy's nftables mode became generally available (GA) in Kubernetes v1.33. The 1.33 changelog says the nftables mode "is now GA", and the 1.37 changelog confirms it became GA in v1.33. The iptables mode stayed the default. You choose nftables with `--proxy-mode nftables` or with `mode: nftables` in a config file.

What came before:
- Alpha in v1.29: a new nftables-based backend was added to kube-proxy. Development had largely shifted from iptables to nftables, some Linux distributions had started deprecating iptables, and nftables claims to solve iptables' main performance problems.
- Beta in v1.31: it sat behind the `NFTablesProxyMode` feature gate, which was now enabled by default. It is Linux-only and requires kernel 5.13 or later. Some behaviours, especially around NodePort services, differ from iptables mode.

The KEP's graduation criteria set the requirements for each step:
- Beta needed at least two releases since alpha, some real-world usage, no major outstanding bugs, and better unit test coverage. It also needed a mode-switching e2e job, a perf/scale job showing performance as good as iptables and ipvs, and documented behaviour differences.
- GA needed at least two releases since beta, non-trivial real-world usage, and no bugs or regressions that would make the maintainers hesitate to recommend it. It also needed the start of a plan for next steps and no UNRESOLVED sections in the KEP.

What came after GA:
- In v1.35, ipvs mode was deprecated, and nftables became the recommended replacement on Linux.
- In v1.37, iptables was still the default. kubeadm now explicitly sets the mode to iptables when it is unset, and kube-proxy warns if the mode isn't set explicitly. This is part of a planned move to nftables as the default in a future release.

answer.question: How did support for multiple Service CIDRs (ServiceCIDR objects) progress through its release stages?
answer.answer:
Multiple Service CIDR support (the MultiCIDRServiceAllocator feature gate, KEP-1880) went through three stages:

1. **Alpha, 1.27–1.30.** The feature gate was off by default.
2. **Beta, 1.31–1.32.** The gate was still off by default. To use the feature, users had to enable the gate and the networking v1beta1 API group. It lets admins change Service CIDR ranges dynamically, with zero downtime.
   - Also in 1.31, the new ClusterIP allocators used a dual-write strategy by default. This avoids duplicate IPs when skewed kube-apiservers run different allocators. Users could opt out with the DisableAllocatorDualWrite gate.
3. **Stable (GA), 1.33 onward.** The gate defaults to true and is locked. In the same release, DisableAllocatorDualWrite moved to beta, off by default. Users can now define the cluster Service CIDR through the ServiceCIDR API object. Admins who want to limit new ServiceCIDRs (for example, keep a single one or stop overlaps) can use ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.

The two versions of the KEP's upgrade/skew section disagree on naming:
- The older, unshipped draft (chunk 24104) calls the default object "ServiceCIDRConfig" and pins the alpha upgrade to 1.25.
- The later shipped KEP text (chunk 24214) uses "ServiceCIDR" and a generic N+1.

The shipped KEP is the lower tier, so it wins. Either way, the feature gate reference shows alpha actually began in 1.27.

answer.question: Why did SIG Network build a new nftables backend for kube-proxy?
answer.answer:
According to the KEP and release material, there were several reasons:

- **iptables is fading out.** The default Linux kube-proxy implementation was based on iptables. Problems with iptables led to its successor, nftables. Development on iptables has mostly stopped, and new features and performance improvements now go mainly into nftables. Some Linux distributions had already started to deprecate and remove iptables, and nftables claims to solve iptables' main performance problems. Doing nothing would eventually leave many users unable to use the default proxy implementation.
- **One backend instead of two.** SIG Network was supporting both the iptables and ipvs backends. It did not feel it could drop ipvs because of perceived iptables performance issues. A backend as functional and non-buggy as iptables but as performant as ipvs could eventually let both existing backends be deprecated, leaving only one Linux backend to support.
- **Performance.** The nftables API allows incremental updates sized only to the Services and endpoints that changed. iptables needs O(n) updates in the total number of Services. Each component also gets a private table, so there is no global lock contention.
- **Cleanup of shared code.** There is a desire for a "kube-proxy library" that third parties could use. Writing a new backend would force a fresh look at the shared core kube-proxy code, with a view to cleaning it up and refactoring it.
- **Existing alternatives didn't fit.** At least three nftables-based implementations already existed (kube-nftlb, nfproxy, kpng's nft backend). None was suitable to adopt directly or to use as a starting point.
